The report highlights the complexity of understanding the sources of information systems, as each component may rely on multiple supply chains and manufacturers located globally. Federal agencies heavily rely on commercially available IT products, many of which are manufactured overseas. The Federal Information Security Modernization Act (FISMA) requires agencies to manage supply chain risks as part of their information security programs. NIST provides guidelines for managing supply chain risks, including conducting due diligence reviews and implementing security controls. The report also mentions several incidents where federal systems were compromised due to supply chain risks, such as the use of Kaspersky products. The report recommends that agencies take steps to better manage supply chain risks, including conducting risk assessments, implementing security controls, and collaborating with other agencies. The report also mentions that several federal agencies have taken steps to improve their management of supply chain risks, but more work is needed. Overall, the report emphasizes the importance of federal agencies managing supply chain risks to protect their information systems and the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the data they handle.

The report by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) examines grant programs awarded by the Departments of Health and Human Services (HHS), Labor (DOL), and Justice (DOJ) from 2007 to 2015 that were subject to statutory restrictions on religious-based hiring. The report identified 2,586 grantees who received funding through at least 53 grant programs, with HHS identifying one grant program, Projects for Assistance in Transition from Homelessness (PATH), where nonprofits could be primary recipients but no faith-based organizations (FBOs) were awarded grants. DOL identified 19 potential FBOs among the grantees, while DOJ identified nine FBOs that self-certified as exempt from statutory restrictions on religious-based hiring. The report also notes that DOL and HHS reported no FBOs sought exemptions, while DOL and HHS did not provide any documentation on the RFRA exemptions. The report concludes that the agencies inform grant applicants of the RFRA exemptions through grant announcements and other methods.
